explanation: The vagal nerve (CN X) exits the skull via the jugular foramen. Its superior (jugular) ganglion gives off only meningeal and auricular branches before the nerve continues inferiorly as the cervical vagus.
keyConcept: Vagal nerve ganglia and extracranial branches

explanation: The thalamus receives arterial blood from perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), specifically the posteromedial (for medial/anterior thalamus) and posterolateral (thalamogeniculate) groups, which are branches of the P2 segment of the PCA.
keyConcept: Thalamic blood supply via PCA branches

explanation: Venous drainage of the thalamus is primarily via the thalamostriate vein (also called the terminal vein), which drains into the internal cerebral vein and subsequently contributes to the vein of Galen.
keyConcept: Thalamic venous drainage via thalamostriate vein

explanation: The lateral ventricle boundaries include: lateral wall (caudate nucleus), medial wall (septum pellucidum), roof (corpus callosum), floor (thalamus and hypothalamus), anterior wall (paraterminal gyrus), and posterior wall (splenium of corpus callosum).

The third ventricle has four recesses: optic recess (between optic chiasma and lamina terminalis), infundibular recess (into the pituitary stalk), pineal recess (into the pineal body), and suprapineal recess (above the pineal body).
keyConcept: Third ventricle recesses and their locations

explanation: The septal areas connect to the hypothalamus via the medial forebrain bundle and to the habenular nuclei via the stria medullaris thalami, forming key components of the limbic circuitry.
keyConcept: Septal area connections and limbic circuitry

explanation: The fornix carries the major output tract of the hippocampus, connecting it to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix, thus completing the Papez circuit involved in memory and emotion.

Lesions to the hippocampus or Papez circuit cause anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) while preserving old memories, reflecting the hippocampus's critical role in memory consolidation.

The limbic lobe consists of a C-shaped ring of cortical tissue including the subcallosal area, cingulate gyrus, isthmus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus, forming the emotional processing center of the brain.

The five major long association fibers are: superior longitudinal fasciculus (connecting frontal to parietal/occipital/temporal), inferior longitudinal fasciculus (temporal to occipital), fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus (frontal to temporal), and cingulum (cingulate to entorhinal cortex).
keyConcept: Long association fibers and their connectivity

explanation: The internal capsule blood supply varies by region: the upper anterior and posterior limbs receive MCA branches; the lower anterior limb and genu receive ACA branches; the lower posterior limb receives the anterior choroidal artery; and the retrolentiform/sublentiform parts receive the anterior choroidal artery.

The corpus callosum is related superiorly to the falx cerebri and anterior cerebral arteries, and inferiorly to the fornix and septum pellucidum, making it a key anatomical landmark in the interhemispheric fissure.
keyConcept: Corpus callosum superior and inferior relations

explanation: The major subarachnoid cisterns include the cerebellomedullary cistern (below cerebellum), cisterna magna (between cerebellum and medulla), pontine cistern, interpeduncular cistern, and cistern of the lateral fossa.

CSF is actively secreted by the choroid plexus epithelial cells in the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles, primarily via Na+/K+ ATPase-driven transport mechanisms producing approximately 500 mL daily.

CSF flows from lateral ventricles through interventricular foramina to third ventricle, then via cerebral aqueduct to fourth ventricle, exiting through median/lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Most CSF is absorbed through arachnoid villi projecting into dural venous sinuses, returning CSF to the bloodstream; a small amount is also absorbed perivascularly around penetrating brain vessels.
The vertebral artery gives off meningeal, posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA), posterior spinal, anterior spinal, and medullary (paramedian) branches as it ascends through the foramen magnum.

The vertebral artery begins as a branch of the first (proximal) part of the subclavian artery and terminates at the lower border of the pons by joining the contralateral vertebral artery to form the basilar artery.

The basilar artery is formed at the lower border of the pons by the union of the two vertebral arteries and terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

The basilar artery gives off pontine (paramedian) branches, labyrinthine artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), superior cerebellar artery (SCA), and its terminal branches the posterior cerebral arteries.

The circle of Willis is formed anteriorly by the anterior cerebral arteries and anterior communicating artery, laterally by the internal carotid arteries and posterior communicating arteries, and posteriorly by the posterior cerebral arteries.

The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere (except occipital lobe), a one-inch strip of the superior lateral surface, and the medial part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral cerebral surface (excluding occipital pole and superior/inferior border strips), the lateral orbital surface, and the temporal pole.
The posterior cerebral artery supplies the medial and lateral occipital surfaces, the inferior temporal surface (except temporal pole), and contributes to the visual cortex via calcarine artery.
Mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage (1st arch) differentiates into malleus, incus, sphenomandibular ligament, anterior ligament of malleus, and contributes to mandibular formation.
Chromaffin cells (neural crest derivatives) give rise to the adrenal medulla, paraganglia (including carotid and aortic bodies), and extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue throughout the body.

The second pharyngeal arch arterial derivative largely regresses, leaving only the stapedial artery; the third arch forms the common carotid artery and the proximal internal carotid artery, with the external carotid arising as a sprout.
The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands (from its inferior wing) and the thymus (from its ventral wing), explaining the common origin of these structures.

The intermaxillary segment (median nasal prominence) gives rise to the philtrum of the upper lip, the primary palate (premaxilla carrying the four incisor teeth), and the median part of the upper jaw.

The five secondary brain vesicles and their adult derivatives are: telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres), diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus), mesencephalon (midbrain), metencephalon (pons and cerebellum), and myelencephalon (medulla oblongata).

Neural crest cells migrate to form sensory ganglia (neuroblasts), autonomic ganglia, melanocytes, chromaffin cells, Schwann cells, meninges (pia and arachnoid), odontoblasts, and skeletal elements of branchial arches.
keyConcept: Neural crest cell derivatives and migration

explanation: The nervous system maintains homeostasis, controls skeletal muscle activity, regulates glandular secretion, processes sensory information, and subserves higher mental functions including consciousness, learning, and memory.

A synapse is a specialized functional junction between two neurons (or a neuron and an effector) where information is transmitted via neurotransmitter release, allowing communication between electrically separate cells.

Synaptic functions include unidirectional impulse transmission, convergence (multiple inputs to one neuron for intensity encoding), divergence (one neuron to multiple targets), and are primary sites of drug action.

Chemical synapses use neurotransmitter release and receptor activation for unidirectional, slower, drug-sensitive transmission; electrical synapses use gap junctions for bidirectional, faster signaling with no drug sensitivity.

Chemical neurotransmission involves calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, ion channel modulation, postsynaptic potential changes, and subsequent neurotransmitter removal via reuptake, degradation, or diffusion.
Neurotransmitters are removed from the synaptic cleft by presynaptic reuptake (active transport), enzymatic degradation at postsynaptic membrane, or passive diffusion away from the synapse.

A neurotransmitter is rapidly inactivated and acts briefly between neurons; a neuromodulator acts more slowly and long-term to alter synaptic effectiveness; a neurohormone is released into blood to act at distant targets.
keyConcept: Distinction between neurotransmitter, neuromodulator, and neurohormone

explanation: Acetylcholine is released at CNS synapses (cortex, thalamus), all neuromuscular junctions, all autonomic preganglionic terminals, all postganglionic parasympathetic terminals, and some sympathetic terminals (sweat glands, skeletal muscle vessels).
keyConcept: Acetylcholine release sites in nervous system

explanation: Norepinephrine is generally excitatory on alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction) and inhibitory on beta-2 receptors (bronchodilation, vasodilation), producing complex tissue-specific effects depending on receptor distribution.
GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through GABA-A receptors to increase chloride ion influx, causing membrane hyperpolarization and neuronal inhibition.

Touch receptors (Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles) are rapidly adapting phasic receptors, while pain receptors (free nerve endings) are slowly adapting tonic receptors, reflecting their functional roles in sensory processing.
keyConcept: Receptor adaptation rates and functional significance
